content: H5N2 is a subtype of the Influenza A virus, commonly referred to as avian influenza or bird flu. A highly pathogenic strain of H5N2 was responsible for significant outbreaks in poultry, leading to substantial economic losses. These outbreaks occurred in 1983 in Pennsylvania, USA, affecting chickens and turkeys; in 1994 in Mexico, primarily in chickens; and a minor outbreak in 1997 in Italy, also in chickens. On November 12, 2005, it was reported that one of two birds infected with avian influenza in Kuwait carried the H5N1 strain of the virus. This bird was a migrating flamingo found on a beach in Kuwait. The other bird, an imported falcon, was found to be infected with the milder H5N2 variant. In China, an inactivated H5N2 strain has been utilized as a vaccine against H5N1. On May 11, 2006, Japan's Health Ministry announced that 93 poultry farm workers near Tokyo might have been exposed to H5N2 in 2005. This strain was not previously known to infect humans. Preliminary tests revealed the presence of H5N2 antibodies in these workers, indicating prior exposure. However, none of the individuals tested positive for the virus itself or exhibited flu-like symptoms. Following H5N2 outbreaks in Ibaraki, Japan, approximately 7 million birds were culled to contain the spread. In 2006, an H5N2 outbreak on a single farm in South Africa led to the culling of all 60 ostriches on the premises. The strain was similar to one that caused outbreaks in South Africa during 2004 and 2005. In 2007, a low-pathogenic strain of H5N2 was detected during routine testing of 25,000 turkeys in Pendleton County, West Virginia, prior to their slaughter. The birds showed no signs of illness or mortality, but measures were implemented to prevent the virus from mutating or spreading. Later in 2007, on December 21, an H5N2 outbreak was identified in the Dominican Republic, specifically in a suburb of Higuey City on the eastern side of the island. Fifteen roosters and two hens were culled despite showing no visible signs of infection.
